rationales.A: The 1930s policy raised tariffs, not lowered them. Background: Smoot-Hawley pushed American tariffs to historic highs, and world trade collapsed in response.
rationales.B: NAFTA was negotiated by the three governments, not written by the United Nations. Background: the agreement was a treaty among the United States, Canada, and Mexico, ratified by each country's legislature.
rationales.C:
The photograph shows a president signing an agreement to remove trade barriers between three nations. Background: the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 did the reverse, raising American tariffs to record levels and deepening the Depression as other nations retaliated.
Protection then, openness now — the two policies point in opposite directions, which is why NAFTA marks a turn in the story.
rationales.D: Both policies covered broad trade, not one sector. Background: Smoot-Hawley raised duties on thousands of goods, and NAFTA removed barriers across farming, manufacturing, and services alike.
rationales.general:
1. Name what the photograph shows. A president signing an agreement that tears down trade barriers.
2. Name the opposite. Background: the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 raised American tariffs to record levels, and other nations answered with tariffs of their own.
3. Compare the directions. One policy opens markets; the other closed them.
4. Ask what the contrast means. In sixty years the United States went from protecting its markets to opening them — the heart of globalization.
Remember: NAFTA is the mirror image of Smoot-Hawley — openness where the 1930s chose walls.

stimulus.text: President Bill Clinton signs the North American Free Trade Agreement into law on December 8, 1993. Standing behind him are three former presidents — Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, and George H. W. Bush — and Vice President Al Gore applauds at the right.
